idiom_name: concept/model wrapper with a hidden interface behind a value handle
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: name the behaviour clients need as a minimal interface (Concept); for every concrete type T with that behaviour, generate a binder (Model<T>) that stores a T and forwards each operation; the public handle is one non-templated value type that owns a binder and forwards to it. Decide the completion protocol explicitly - destruction through the interface, clone when the handle is copyable, move semantics, and a defined empty state. Bind at construction or through a factory, because that is the only place the concrete type appears, and dispatch at use. Where the language performs the erasure itself (interfaces, trait objects, existentials, dynamic typing), prefer that native mechanism and hand-roll only the general case the platform does not provide.
code_sketch:
interface Concept:                       # erased behaviour, hidden from clients
    op_1(); op_2(); clone(); destroy()

class Model<T> implements Concept:      # one instantiation per concrete type
    value: T
    op_1() { value.op_1() }             # forward as-is

class Handle:                           # non-templated, value-semantic
    binder: Concept
    Handle(T x) { binder = Model<T>(x) }  # binding: the only place T is known
    op_1() { binder.op_1() }              # dispatch: T unknown from here on
pitfalls: Omitting destruction or clone from the concept: deleting or copying through the erased interface is then undefined, not merely unavailable.
Binding in a non-template constructor, or storing a reference or pointer to a temporary, so the erased value outlives what it points at.
Letting the concrete type leak back into the public API (a template method or a getter), which reintroduces the coupling the wrapper removed.

Wrong move: assuming erasure is allocation-free because the wrapper has small-buffer storage -> values past the inline budget silently heap-allocate and the budget shifts with the standard-library version -> treat one allocation plus one indirect call as the expected cost and rely on inline storage only as a measured optimisation.

Wrong move: erasing below the module boundary and calling erased operations in hot loops -> witness-table/vtable dispatch defeats inlining and the closed local type set pays indirection for openness it never uses -> keep generics (templates, some P, <T>) inside the module and erase only at the API boundary where the concrete types must differ.

Wrong move: binding a trait or protocol to an existential before checking it can be erased -> a trait with generic or Self-returning methods is not dyn-compatible (object-unsafe) and the failure surfaces at the least convenient call site -> check dyn-compatibility/protocol constraints first, then fall back to an enum, a generic, or a hand-rolled Concept/Model wrapper that lifts the restriction.
